info.bio:
Black Sabbath oriundos de Birmingham, Reino Unido con un sonido característico y único en su especie, emergió como una propuesta hacia finales de los años 60, siendo el ensamble musical pionero del sonido más disruptivo del planeta.
La banda se formó en 1968, compuesta por el cantante John Ozzy Osbourne, el guitarrista Frank Anthony Tony Iommi, el bajista Terence Geezer Butler y el baterista William Bill Ward.

own_scenes.desc: Con Led Zeppelin, la banda fundadora del heavy según la mayoría (los británicos la prefieren a ella). Se llamaban Earth, un nombre hippie, hasta que una confusión con una banda de cabaret los mandó a tocar a una fiesta que esperaba valses; adoptaron el título de una película de terror de Boris Karloff, que ya era el de una de sus canciones, como corrección expresa del «paz y amor». Geezer Butler cuenta que un crítico americano describió su música hacia 1972 como «el sonido del heavy metal estrellándose». Su gira se anunciaba como «más ruidosa que Led Zeppelin»; abrían para ellos Yes, Alice Cooper o los Ramones. Su tema más famoso sobre drogas, «Sweet Leaf», es más psicodélico que heavy; «Iron Man» es uno de los monstruos favoritos del metal y «Children of the Grave», una canción contra la guerra atómica.

refs.para: In his social history of rock music, Loyd Grossman referred to the genre of heavy metal as “Downer Rock,” commenting that its “chief exponents were Black Sabbath, a thuggy, atavistic, and philosophically lugubrious British quartet who became quite successful performing songs about paranoia, World War HI, and other whistle-a-happy-tune subjects.”¹²
refs.chapter: Cap. 1: Estudiar el metal: el bricolage de la cultura

refs.q: Black Sabbath’s name, adopted by the group in 1969, is paradigmatic for heavy metal.
refs.para: Led Zeppelin’s name also was not related to the genre of heavy metal. The group, formed by Jimmy Page after his departure from the Yardbirds, was originally called the New Yardbirds. According to legend, the Who’s irrepressible drummer, Keith Moon, heard them and was not impressed. Their music would go down “like a lead zeppelin,” he prophesied. Black Sabbath’s name, adopted by the group in 1969, is paradigmatic for heavy metal. The band’s original name was Earth, reflecting a hippie aesthetic. However, Earth was also the name of a cabaret band and booking agents tended to mistake the bands for one another. After a booking mistake that sent them to a business party at which the audience expected waltzes, the frustrated band members renamed themselves with the title of a song they had just written. Black Sabbath was the name of a British horror movie, starring Boris Karloff.⁴¹ They expressly chose the new name to be a corrective to the “peace and love” credo that permeated the youth culture at the time.⁴²
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Heavy metal: la bestia que se niega a morir

refs.q: Black Sabbath’s tour in the early 1970s was touted by the record company as “Louder Than Led Zeppelin.”
refs.para: The essential sonic element in heavy metal is power, expressed as sheer volume. Loudness is meant to overwhelm, to sweep the listener into the sound, and then to lend the listener the sense of power that the sound provides. Injunctions such as “crank it up,” “turn it up,” and “blow your speakers” fill the lyrics of heavy metal songs. Black Sabbath’s tour in the early 1970s was touted by the record company as “Louder Than Led Zeppelin.”³⁰ At concerts the stage is loaded with stacks of amplifiers so that the decibel level of the instruments can be raised to the limit. The sonic standards of the concert are replicated in recordings. The kind of power that loudness gives is a shot of youthful vitality, a power to withstand the onslaught of sound and to expand one’s energy to respond to it with a physical and emotional thrust of one’s own. Heavy metal’s loudness is not deafening, irritating, or painful (at least to the fan), but empowering. It is not just a “wall of sound,” as detractors complain: it is an often complicated sonic pattern played out in high volume.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Heavy metal: la bestia que se niega a morir

refs.q: The most famous drug song in heavy metal is Black Sabbath’s “Sweet Leaf,”
refs.para: The second member of the trinity of sex, drugs, and rock and roll does not fare so well in the lyrics of heavy metal. Despite the use of drugs by many members of heavy metal’s audience and the celebration of drugs in psychedelic music, heavy metal has avoided the theme, perhaps because it does not resonate with the power of the music the way physical sex does. The most famous drug song in heavy metal is Black Sabbath’s “Sweet Leaf,” which was written at a time when marijuana use among youth in the West was at a peak. Appearing on Sabbath’s 1971 album Master of Reality, the song celebrates marijuana for allowing one to know one’s own mind. This lyric is not consistent with heavy metal’s sensibility, but instead expresses the aesthetic of psychedelic music.⁴⁶ The few rousing drinking songs in heavy metal are, however, thoroughly Dionysian. Saxon’s “Party Til You Puke” and W.A.S.P.’s “Blind in Texas” are wild musical and lyrical paeans to getting crazy drunk.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Heavy metal: la bestia que se niega a morir

refs.q: Black Sabbath’s “Children of the Grave” is about the death that will be brought by atomic warfare if the battle for peace is not won.
refs.para: The extreme reaction of the weak and vulnerable to chaos, external or internal, is suicide and death itself. Death is the extinguishing of relations. Since order means relationship among things, death is ultimate chaos. Judas Priest’s “Beyond the Realms of Death” describes the despair of someone cut off from the world. Venomously, the person defends his decision to cut himself off from the living. It is his escape from a world so full of “sin” that it is “not worth living in.” Black Sabbath’s “Children of the Grave” is about the death that will be brought by atomic warfare if the battle for peace is not won. This focus on vulnerability to the horrors of chaos is a very significant feature of traditional heavy metal. It became the centerpiece of thrash metal in the late 1980s.

scenes.name: El oficio: del air guitar al dios del metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El músico de heavy sale del público: es el fan que toca la guitarra de aire en el concierto de UFO de 1979 y quiere estar donde está Michael Schenker. No hay escuela ni beca: hace falta talento musical y dramático (actuar la emoción por trescientas veces), un cuerpo joven y atlético (correr y pesas en la gira, el pelo largo como signo de autenticidad) y aprender a vivir en un grupo que no es ni familia ni oficina, con sus «problemas de ego» por la rivalidad entre cantante y guitarrista. El heavy es el estilo más caro de montar y casi no hay clubes donde empezar; el código exige temas propios y autenticidad. Firmar con un sello convierte a la banda en una empresa del capitalismo tardío frente a un oligopolio. El ciclo es componer, grabar (paciencia; el primer disco de Black Sabbath se hizo en doce horas, Spreading the Disease de Anthrax en cinco meses) y girar (aguante: esperar, esperar). La recompensa no es el dinero sino el carisma del chamán que alcanza el éxtasis dionisíaco ante miles de personas; el precio, «quemarse o apagarse», porque nadie que viva lo bastante puede cumplir el código.

scenes.name: La radio: del exilio a Z-Rock
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Durante su primera década el heavy casi no suena en la radio: la FM progresiva rechaza a Black Sabbath por cambiar «love» por «evil», el AOR de los consultores solo pone «Stairway to Heaven» y algo de AC/DC, y a los anunciantes no les interesan los chicos de quince a dieciocho años. Weinstein ve ventajas en ese exilio: obliga a las bandas a girar sin parar (Aerosmith, Blue Öyster Cult y Ted Nugent, más de cuarenta semanas al año), las une a su público, las libra de los códigos radiofónicos (canciones de ocho minutos como «War Pigs», solos largos, el disco y no el single como unidad) y explica la abundancia de discos en directo. En los ochenta llegan los programas de metal en las radios universitarias (WSOU de Seton Hall se pasa entera al metal), el informe metal de CMJ y su Metal Marathon, y en la radio comercial el formato por satélite Z-Rock desde Dallas, que relega el thrash a su «Headbanger’s Heaven» nocturno. En Gran Bretaña, el único refugio es el «Friday Night Rock Show» de la BBC con Tommy Vance. Cuando la radio comercial acepta el metal es a través de MTV y de las power ballads, y exige productores de éxitos y solos recortados; aun así Metallica vende un millón de …And Justice for All sin apenas sonar.

scenes.name: Conciertos y festivales: Donington y el negocio de la gira
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El concierto es, con el disco, el medio que siempre ha formado parte del metal y el más fiel a la relación entre artista y público. En los setenta los conciertos de heavy son un negocio seguro: llenan sin promoción y su público, pese al aspecto de Hell’s Angels, es fácil de manejar (los vigilantes de Chicago lo prefieren al de la música country). Hacia 1978 Black Sabbath, Rainbow, Judas Priest y UFO llenan grandes recintos, que necesitan mucho volumen y asientos sin tapizar. En los primeros ochenta llegan los festivales de metal como el de Donington, y tras el US Festival de 1983 el negocio florece: clubes dedicados, estadios al aire libre, festivales europeos de más de cien mil personas, patrocinio de cerveza y tabaco y el merchandising, que controla la banda y por el que ahora se sale de gira.

scenes.name: La «muerte» del metal en los noventa
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: A mediados de los noventa se expide el certificado de defunción del metal, y hay varios sospechosos. Para los headbangers fue una puñalada de Metallica: el disco homónimo de 1991, lleno de baladas radiables, Load y ReLoad, el cartel de Lollapalooza y la portada de Rolling Stone con pelo corto, eyeliner y piercings. Otros culpan al grunge, que destrona al lite metal justo cuando Skid Row, Mötley Crüe, Van Halen y Guns N’ Roses debutaban en el número uno en 1991. Pero los grandes grupos también se oxidan: Black Sabbath lleva quince años de cambios de cantante (Dehumanizer con Dio en 1992 y luego solo queda Tony Iommi), Ozzy anuncia que se retira y se desretira, Judas Priest queda inerte tras Painkiller cuando Halford se marcha a Fight y lo ven como un Judas, Bruce Dickinson deja Iron Maiden en 1993. Los fans se consuelan con bandas tributo y discos de homenaje (Nativity in Black, 1994), y el último clavo del ataúd es el disco de versiones melódicas de Pat Boone, In a Metal Mood.

scenes.name: La bestia ha vuelto: OzzFest y las reuniones
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: A finales de siglo el metal vuelve a la corriente principal. Con el alternativo moribundo y la electrónica sin despegar, el público fiel sigue ahí: tres mil personas esperan cinco horas en un centro comercial de Chicago en 1998 a que Black Sabbath les firme discos. El detonante es el OzzFest de 1997, organizado por la mánager de Ozzy, que vende más que Lollapalooza con Pantera, Machine Head, Fear Factory, Type O Negative, Neurosis, tres cuartas partes de Black Sabbath y Marilyn Manson, cuyas provocaciones atraen protestas cristianas y titulares. Metallica vuelve a tocar su thrash en directo y en Garage Inc.; Judas Priest ficha a Tim «Ripper» Owens, cantante de una banda tributo llamada British Steel; Mötley Crüe recupera a Vince Neil, Kiss se reúne en 1998, Dickinson regresa a Iron Maiden y Black Sabbath hace en 1999 una gira de reunión con disco de oro. Weinstein ve en ese regreso el gusto «prole» de la cultura de fin de siglo, un contrapeso a la feminización del pop y la ansiedad milenarista: la bestia se niega a morir.

scenes.name: Hard rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El hard rock marca el fin de los creativos sesenta: sigue basado en el blues, pero más rápido, ruidoso y fuerte, y entierra el sufrimiento negro bajo miles de decibelios. Precedido por Cream, Blue Cheer y Guess Who, lo definen Led Zeppelin, hijos del blues que lo tocan como música para el cuerpo y que imponen el LP como formato del rock. En Gran Bretaña, Free, Status Quo, Thin Lizzy, UFO, Uriah Heep, Slade, Faces, Deep Purple (el estereotipo del género), Black Sabbath (cimientos del black y el doom metal) y Queen, los bromistas del movimiento. En EE UU, Mountain, James Gang, Grand Funk Railroad, Montrose, Bachman-Turner Overdrive y Heart.

podcast.title: Band Name Origin (1963)
podcast.body: While rehearsing in Birmingham, England, across from a cinema playing a 1963 horror movie titled "Black Sabbath," bassist Geezer Butler observed people paying good money to be scared. This sparked the idea for the band to create music that would also scare and shock people, leading them to rename themselves from "Earth" to "Black Sabbath" after the movie. "One day they noticed that the cinema was playing a 1963 horror movie entitled Black Sabbath."

podcast.body: Black Sabbath's emergence in 1970 is considered the official beginning of heavy metal, primarily because they introduced not only a new way of playing and tuning instruments but also a distinct thematic and aesthetic approach. This comprehensive artistic vision became a fundamental pillar of the heavy metal movement. podcast.body: In 1978, eight years after establishing a consistent following, Ozzy Osbourne clarified that Black Sabbath was not a satanic band. He stated their dark imagery and themes were a deliberate strategy to "create a brand to sell the band," indicating a calculated marketing approach rather than genuine occult beliefs. "In 1978, Ozzy Osborne said that black Sabbath was not a satanic band, and that they were really just trying to quote, create a brand to sell the band."

xref.body: Chris Sangerides, a Greek Cypriot, was chosen to produce *Fully Completely*. He was known for his work with heavy metal acts like Judas Priest, Black Sabbath, Ozzy, and Thin Lizzy, but The Tragically Hip were primarily drawn to the sound of records he produced for Concrete Blonde. The band felt disarmed by his lovely demeanor, and he showed his enthusiasm by traveling to Toronto to see them play at the Horseshoe Tavern before recording. Sangerides implemented a traditional 1970s recording technique, which was "completely alien" to the band's usual live-style approach, focusing on building tracks from the bass and drums upwards. xref.title: Development of Signature Sound
xref.body: Due to his finger injury and the use of thimbles, Iommi found soloing tough and concentrated on playing heavy power chords. He couldn't bend standard guitar strings well, so he used banjo strings and tuned his guitar low to C sharp (drop C sharp) to make them looser and easier to play. This combination of techniques—heavy power chords, banjo strings, and low tuning—created the distinctive heavy, sinister, and powerful guitar sound that made Black Sabbath famous and significantly contributed to the sound of heavy metal. "Put this all together, and you have the distinctive guitar sound that made his band, Black Sabbath, famous."

xref.title: Hip-Hop Influence on Guitar Style
xref.body: Despite playing in bands that covered rock acts like Led Zeppelin, Bachman-Turner Overdrive, and Black Sabbath, Tom Morello was profoundly influenced by Run DMC and Public Enemy. xref.title: Popularization of Devil Horns Gesture
xref.body: Ronnie James Dio popularized the "devil horns" gesture, learning it from his Italian grandmother who called it the "Malocchio," used to ward off or give the evil eye. xref.title: Producer for The Tragically Hip's Fully Completely
xref.body: Chris Sangerides, a Greek Cypriot, produced The Tragically Hip's *Fully Completely*. He was known for working with heavy metal bands such as Judas Priest, Black Sabbath, Ozzy, and Thin Lizzy, but The Hip were specifically impressed by his work with Concrete Blonde. Sangerides was enthusiastic about producing *Fully Completely*, traveling to Toronto to see the band perform live before committing. He introduced a "traditional 1970s recording" approach, which was initially "completely alien" to The Hip, by stripping everything down and building tracks from the bass and drums up over three weeks, which resulted in a bigger, more isolated sound. "Chris really wanted to strip everything down in a way that I think is much more traditional 1970s recording, but for us it was completely alien."

xref.title: Terry Chimes' Career Change to Healthcare
xref.body: After a successful music career with The Clash, Generation X, and Black Sabbath, Terry Chimes began to rethink his path in the late 1980s. Influenced by his experiences with the rock and roll lifestyle, he concluded that "the natural way of healing is far better than pumping people full of drugs." This led him to adopt a meat- and alcohol-free lifestyle, study chiropractic medicine at various schools across the UK, and learn acupuncture in China. "But by the end of the 1980s, Terry began thinking about doing something else."
